name: LSQUIC (LiteSpeed QUIC)
workload: HTTP/3 download of an 8GB file over a 10Gbit/s link between two dedicated bare-metal hosts, using an extended QUIC Interop Runner; all client/server pairs across 6 QUIC libraries measured, 50 repetitions per pair.
claimed_speedup: LSQUIC-LSQUIC pair: 3004 Mbit/s vs quiche-quiche pair: 2506 Mbit/s (~1.2x, derived from page data, Fig. 3); with 32x larger UDP receive buffers and architecture-tuned compile flags, LSQUIC*-LSQUIC*: 3882 Mbit/s vs quiche*-quiche*: 2590 Mbit/s (~1.5x, derived from page data, Fig. 10)
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the baseline pairs (example/default builds of each project were used); optimized variants (LSQUIC*/quiche*) used unspecified 'compile flags to optimize for the used architecture' (exact flags not given in the paper text extracted)
hardware: Default: AMD EPYC 7543 (32-core), Broadcom BCM57416 NIC, Debian Bullseye, kernel 5.10.0-8-amd64. Also repeated on AMD EPYC 7551P, Intel Xeon D-1518, Intel Xeon E5-1650, Intel Xeon Gold 6312U (paper Table I).
tradeoffs: Goodput is highly asymmetric by client/server combination: in this same study the quiche-server/LSQUIC-client pair reaches more than 2x the goodput of the LSQUIC-server/quiche-client pair, so the 'LSQUIC beats quiche' result holds for matched same-vendor pairs, not universally across mixed pairs. LSQUIC showed unintended retransmission behavior with BBR congestion control in this study (paper forced Cubic/Reno for all libraries to keep the comparison fair).
caveats: Peer-reviewed (IFIP Networking 2023 / EPIQ lineage, ISBN 978-3-903176-57-7) and the measurement framework + configs + results are published (github.com/tumi8/quic-10g-paper, confirmed the CPU table matches the paper), but the paper text itself does not state the compiler or exact compile flags for the baseline (non-optimized) pairs, so this is capped at Tier B rather than A.
found_via: arXiv API search_query=all:QUIC AND all:implementation AND all:performance -> arxiv.org/abs/2309.16395 'QUIC on the Highway: Evaluating Performance on High-rate Links'

name: LSQUIC-DPDK (tumi8 kernel-bypass fork)
workload: HTTP/3 large-file download between two bare-metal hosts, DPDK+SR-IOV kernel-bypass builds of each QUIC library, same-implementation client/server pairs, 50 repetitions each (measurement-data/06-dpdk-integration).
claimed_speedup: LSQUIC-DPDK (SR-IOV) pair averaged 11019 Mbit/s vs MsQuic-DPDK (SR-IOV) pair averaging 8118 Mbit/s (~1.36x); also beats quiche-DPDK (SR-IOV) pair averaging 6168 Mbit/s (~1.79x) in the same table (derived from page data)
hardware: Bare-metal server pair; NIC using the Intel 'ice' driver (E810 family) with SR-IOV. Exact CPU model not found in the repository content inspected this session.
stars_or_usage: 0 stars (research artifact accompanying a NOMS 2026 paper)
tradeoffs: Same DPDK/SR-IOV deployment complexity as other entries in this family (dedicated NIC/queue, hugepages, root). A separate table in the same dataset (measurement-data/01-implementation-matrix/processed.csv) shows msquic-dpdk NOT beating vanilla kernel msquic (7982 vs 8250 Mbit/s), so DPDK's benefit is very implementation-dependent; only the head-to-head DPDK-vs-DPDK cross-library comparison used here is a clean win for LSQUIC-DPDK.
caveats: Same unpublished-paper caveat as the quiche-DPDK entry above (DOI TODO, NOMS 2026); numbers come straight from the group's published CSV rather than paper prose. Treat the ratio as directional given some inconsistency between the two published data tables for msquic-dpdk.
found_via: Same discovery path as quiche-DPDK entry: gh api orgs/tumi8/repos -> tumi8/quic-bypass-paper -> measurement-data/06-dpdk-integration/processed.csv

name: quiche-DPDK (tumi8 kernel-bypass fork)
language: C (DPDK kernel-bypass I/O layer added on top of upstream Rust quiche core)
workload: HTTP/3 large-file download between two bare-metal hosts using an extended QUIC Interop Runner framework; vanilla kernel-socket quiche-quiche pair vs DPDK-kernel-bypass quiche-dpdk-quiche-dpdk pair, 50 repetitions each.
claimed_speedup: ~1.83x goodput: quiche-quiche (kernel) pair averaged 3241 Mbit/s vs quiche-dpdk-quiche-dpdk pair averaging 5937 Mbit/s (derived from page data: measurement-data/01-implementation-matrix/processed.csv)
hardware: Bare-metal server pair; NIC using the Intel 'ice' driver (E810 family) per framework/testbed/testbed_stoi-pact.json. Exact CPU model not found in the repository content inspected this session (paper not yet formally published: DOI listed as TODO, venue NOMS 2026).
stars_or_usage: 0 stars (research artifact accompanying a NOMS 2026 paper)
tradeoffs: DPDK requires dedicating a whole NIC/queue to userspace polling (no shared use with the kernel network stack), hugepages, and root/elevated privileges; adds substantial deployment complexity vs a drop-in library. No license file found in this repo (upstream quiche is Apache-2.0/BSD-2-Clause), so treat the fork's own additions as 'look but don't copy' pending clarification from the authors.
caveats: Numbers are derived directly from the research group's own published raw CSV (dataset mirrored on Zenodo, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.18630971), not from the camera-ready paper text (README lists the paper DOI as TODO; presented at NOMS 2026). CPU model and exact compiler flags were not found in the parts of the repo inspected this session. The same group's prior, closely related methodology (QUIC on the Highway) was peer-reviewed at IFIP Networking 2023.
found_via: gh api orgs/tumi8/repos (listing) -> tumi8/quiche-dpdk README pointing to paper 'Kernel Bypass Surgery: A Viable Procedure for Maximizing QUIC Bandwidth?' -> gh api repos/tumi8/quic-bypass-paper and its measurement-data CSVs

A companion experiments repo (UCLouvain-ENSG/picoquic-dpdk-experiments) is explicitly set up to compare it against quicly, quiche, and msquic directly, but the specific numeric results for those comparisons could not be retrieved this session.

name: mTCP
workload: Short-lived TCP connection handling / small-message request-response transactions on multicore Linux, plus ported applications (e.g. lighttpd) comparing the user-level mTCP stack to the stock Linux TCP stack.
claimed_speedup: up to 25x faster than the latest Linux TCP stack for small-message transactions; ~3x faster than the best-performing prior user-level TCP research system; 33% to 320% throughput improvement for ported applications
tradeoffs: Requires a dedicated packet-I/O driver (DPDK, PacketShader, or netmap) and cores reserved for the mTCP stack; exposes its own epoll-like API rather than drop-in POSIX sockets, so applications must be ported.
caveats: NSDI 2014 best-paper-winning peer-reviewed paper, but the page/PDF text extracted via WebFetch did not surface the exact CPU model or compiler flags, so tier is capped at B rather than A. The paper names the baseline generically as 'the Linux TCP stack'; epoll is inferred as the specific mechanism being beaten via the ported comparison applications (e.g. lighttpd), not quoted verbatim in the abstract.
found_via: USENIX NSDI 2014 presentation page https://www.usenix.org/conference/nsdi14/technical-sessions/presentation/jeong

name: Arrakis
baseline: epoll (well-tuned Linux network stack, Redis-like persistent NoSQL store)
workload: Persistent NoSQL key-value store (Redis-like) request latency and throughput, Arrakis split-kernel OS vs a well-tuned Linux implementation.
claimed_speedup: 2-5x lower latency and up to 9x higher throughput vs a well-tuned Linux implementation
tradeoffs: Requires a custom split-kernel OS (Barrelfish-derived) and virtualized/SR-IOV-capable NIC hardware; not portable to stock Linux; no public source release found.
caveats: OSDI 2014 peer-reviewed paper, but no public code repository was found (checked GitHub), so per the 'papers with no code' rule the tier is capped at C despite peer review. 'Well-tuned Linux implementation' is the paper's own wording; epoll usage by the comparison Redis-like store is inferred, not quoted verbatim in the retrieved abstract/summary.
found_via: USENIX OSDI 2014 presentation page https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi14/technical-sessions/presentation/peter

name: io_uring hybrid storage I/O architecture (Oracle Database)
workload: TPC-C (OLTP) and TPC-H (analytical) database I/O workloads, plus an isolated write-path microbenchmark, comparing io_uring-based storage I/O to the prior libaio-based path in Oracle Database at production scale.
claimed_speedup: OLTP (TPC-C): identical throughput with server CPU utilization reduced by 1.2 percentage points; TPC-H: CPU per query drops 8.5% (geomean); isolated write-path: 29% lower CPU per write and 34% higher throughput; synchronous reads at very large I/O sizes show no improvement or a regression
tradeoffs: Findings are architecture/design guidance embedded in a proprietary closed-source RDBMS, not a reusable open library; benefit is workload-dependent and regresses for very large synchronous reads.
caveats: First-party benchmark by Oracle Database engineers evaluating their own closed-source product; hardware and compiler/build details were not surfaced on the arXiv abstract page; the paper references artifacts at a Zenodo DOI, but the database source itself is not public.
found_via: arXiv API query all:io_uring AND all:asynchronous AND all:performance -> https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22781v1

name: io_uring-echo-server (frevib)
workload: TCP echo server requests/second vs number of concurrent clients (1-1000) and message sizes (128/512/1000 bytes), using the rust_echo_bench load generator, comparing a minimal io_uring (IORING_FEAT_FAST_POLL) echo server against a minimal epoll echo server by the same author
claimed_speedup: 128-byte messages: io_uring peaks at 216,637 req/s (300 clients) vs epoll peak 152,561 req/s (150 clients), ~1.4x; at 1000 clients: io_uring 173,343 vs epoll 108,380 req/s, ~1.6x
compiler_and_flags: Benchmark client (rust_echo_bench) built with `cargo run --release`; the C echo servers are built with `make` and server-side compiler flags are not stated
hardware: MacBook Pro 6-core 2.6GHz host running a VMware Ubuntu 18.04 guest with 6 vCPUs (3 physical cores), 2 cores isolated via isolcpus for the echo server, Linux 5.6.0-rc1+ with IORING_FEAT_FAST_POLL
stars_or_usage: 400 stars; widely cited as a reference io_uring-vs-epoll benchmark (referenced on Hacker News/Twitter)
tradeoffs: At the time of writing, the io_uring echo server needed a per-connection buffer indexed by file descriptor number (segfault risk at high fd counts) and became unresponsive under sustained load with >2000 clients; the epoll counterpart did not show these issues
caveats: Both implementations were written by the same author (not a fully independent third party) specifically to isolate epoll vs io_uring; exact CPU model and C-side compiler flags are not stated; the benchmark is from 2020 on an early io_uring kernel patch (5.6.0-rc1+, pre-mainline IORING_FEAT_FAST_POLL), so it may not reflect current io_uring/liburing performance.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos topic:io-uring -> frevib/io_uring-echo-server README -> benchmarks/benchmarks.md; corroborated via HN Algolia ("io_uring vs epoll: echo server benchmarks")

name: monoio
workload: Extreme-performance TCP test on ByteDance production network: fixed number of client connections against 4 server cores / 16 client cores, 1KB messages, comparing io_uring (Monoio), io_uring (Glommio) and epoll (Tokio) runtimes
claimed_speedup: Monoio peak ~810,075 QPS vs Tokio (epoll) peak ~434,565 QPS (~1.86x) and vs Glommio (io_uring) peak ~603,016 QPS (~1.34x) at 4 server cores

hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 5118 @ 2.30GHz, Intel X710 10GbE NIC, Linux 5.15.4-arch1-1
tradeoffs: Thread-per-core, non-Send/Sync design (values do not escape thread on await); at very low connection counts on a single core, Monoio's io_uring submission latency is higher than Tokio's epoll path, so Tokio wins that narrow case
caveats: First-party benchmark authored by the Monoio maintainers, not an independent suite, though hardware, kernel and rust toolchain versions are stated and raw numeric data is published; test dates from late 2021 on an early io_uring-era kernel (5.15), so results may not reflect current io_uring/epoll performance.

name: UCall
baseline: FastAPI/uvicorn (Python, asyncio - typically epoll-based event loop on Linux)
workload: JSON-RPC round-trip: single-client latency and 32-client throughput on AWS c7g.metal (Graviton3), Ubuntu 22.10, Linux kernel 5.19
claimed_speedup: UCall with io_uring (C): 22us latency / 231,000 rps vs FastAPI over REST: 1,203us / 3,184 rps (~55x latency, ~72x throughput); vs FastAPI over WebSocket: 86us / 11,356 rps (~3.9x latency, ~20x throughput)

A cleaner internal comparison exists in the same table: UCall's own 'POSIX' backend (src/engine_posix.cpp, blocking per-thread accept/recv, not epoll) does 62us/79,000 rps vs UCall's io_uring backend (src/engine_uring.cpp) at 22us/231,000 rps (~2.8x), but that baseline is blocking sockets, not epoll, so it was not used as the primary claim.

name: picohttpparser AVX2 fork (vkrasnov)
workload: Single-threaded req/s over two request corpora: pico's own bench.c request and fukamachi/fast-http's benchmark request (fukamachi.c), comparing the original PCMPESTRI (SSE4.2) token-matching path against a new AVX2+BMI2 bitmask path processing 128 bytes at a time.
hardware: Intel Haswell i5-4278U, turbo disabled for consistency
license: MIT OR Artistic-1.0-Perl (dual-licensed, inherited unchanged from upstream h2o/picohttpparser)
stars_or_usage: 20 stars (fork); submitted as h2o/picohttpparser PR #10, left open/unmerged until closed 2020-07-17

caveats: Benchmark is from 2014 (gcc 4.9.2, Haswell laptop CPU) so absolute numbers are over a decade old, though methodology (CPU model, compiler, flags, public code) is fully specified, meeting tier A. PR was never merged into h2o/picohttpparser and the fork has had no commits since 2014.

name: picohttpparser-rs
workload: Interleaved same-session microbenchmark (scripts/bench_compare.sh / bench_compare.c) timing a safe-Rust reimplementation vs the pinned C picohttpparser (commit f4d94b48) across 8 workload categories: tiny, typical (~400B), large headers (~4.9KB), response (~150B), chunked decode, malformed input, streaming (8 staged prefixes), and an 'upstream marker' (~620B, 11 headers) request.
claimed_speedup: Rust/C time ratio per category: large headers 0.680 (Rust ~32% faster), upstream marker (~620B/11 headers) 0.827 (Rust ~17% faster, flagged 'stability: CHECK'); but streaming 1.023 (near parity), typical 1.100, response 1.185, chunked 1.199, tiny 1.482, malformed 1.811 (all losses for Rust). Author also states native C with -march=native/pcmpestri beats scalar Rust by 1.45x, and -O3 regresses the Rust malformed-path result by 1.68x vs -O2.
compiler_and_flags: C oracle: gcc, default anchor flag -O2 (override via C_OPT env var, e.g. -O3 for labeled side runs); Rust: cargo build --release (rustc 1.96.1)
hardware: Intel Core i5-12400F, single machine, no CPU pinning, whole-loop timer (no p50/p95/p99)
tradeoffs: Rust only wins on 2 of 8 published workloads (large headers, upstream marker); it loses on the other 6, including a 1.8x fixed-cost floor on malformed/reject-fast input. No SIMD path yet ('SIMD prize' explicitly parked/unimplemented), so it cannot match C built with -march=native + PCMPESTRI. Real-consumer integration (H2O/Plack/Furl) is parked, not done.
caveats: Single machine, no CPU pinning, whole-loop timer, explicitly 'not portable' numbers per the author. Extremely new (2 stars, days old at capture time). Most workloads are losses for Rust; only cited here because 2 of the 8 published rows are genuine wins over the named baseline, which the README itself highlights alongside the losses.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "picohttpparser" --sort updated -> logicpl4gue/picohttpparser-rs

name: httpp
workload: Single-threaded repeated parse of picohttpparser's own classic sample GET request (image request with UA/cookie headers), 10,000,000 iterations x 5 runs, averaged.
claimed_speedup: At -O3: httppv2 (2.0.0) 8,893,776.12 req/s vs picohttpparser 3,939,350.39 req/s (~2.26x faster); httppv1 (1.0.0) 2,855,841.74 req/s, actually slower than pico at -O3. At -O0: httppv1 2,008,030.68 req/s and httppv2 3,475,424.44 req/s both beat picohttpparser's 1,130,465.28 req/s.
hardware: Ryzen 7, ~4.79GHz peak frequency (exact SKU not given)
tradeoffs: Header-only C, fixed-size stack-allocated header array, no SIMD (wins via lower per-call overhead, not vectorization). Only the v2.0.0 variant beats picohttpparser at -O3; v1.0.0 is slower at -O3 despite winning at -O0.
caveats: CPU stated only as family ('Ryzen 7'), not exact model/SKU, so capped below tier A. Benchmark request text is adapted directly from picohttpparser's own README example. Very new, single-maintainer, low-star project.
found_via: GitHub: gh search code "picohttpparser" "benchmark" -> cebem1nt/httpp benchmarks/bench-pico.c

name: hparse
workload: poop benchmark (like hyperfine, with hardware counters) repeatedly running standalone parse binaries for picohttpparser, httparse (Rust), and hparse (Zig) over an HTTP/1.1 request; measures wall time, CPU cycles, instructions retired, cache references/misses, branch misses.
claimed_speedup: hparse: 1.27s wall-time / 5.38G cpu_cycles / 8.01G instructions vs picohttpparser: 1.45s wall-time / 6.16G cpu_cycles / 34.7G instructions (~12.5% faster wall-clock, ~12.6% fewer cycles, ~77% fewer instructions retired); also beats httparse (Rust) at 1.54s wall-time / 6.53G cycles.
compiler_and_flags: zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast (hparse); cargo build --release (httparse); picohttpparser built via its own upstream Makefile with default flags (bench/Makefile)
tradeoffs: Zig-only public API (needs a C shim for direct C++ linkage); streaming/never-allocates design explicitly modeled after picohttpparser so it can be 'swapped in smoothly'. A separate skylake-tuned build target exists (-Dcpu=skylake) but its numbers are not published.
caveats: No CPU model or OS/kernel stated for the benchmark host, so methodology is partial despite public benchmark code and stated compiler flags -> capped at tier C, not A/B. Single-host, unspecified-hardware numbers.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos --topic http-parser --sort stars -> nikneym/hparse

name: EverCrypt (HACL*) Curve25519 (Vale-optimized)
workload: Curve25519 scalar multiplication (the ECDH key exchange used in TLS 1.3), cycle count per operation, measured with a Linux kernel crypto benchmarking suite
claimed_speedup: EverCrypt's targeted (Vale-assembly) Curve25519 implementation narrowly exceeds OpenSSL's by ~3% (also ~1% faster than Oliveira et al.'s hand-written asm and ~22% faster than Erbsen et al./fiat-crypto's verified C)
benchmark_url: https://project-everest.github.io/assets/evercrypt.pdf (Figure 9, 'EverCrypt: A Fast, Verified, Cross-Platform Cryptographic Provider', IEEE S&P 2020)
stars_or_usage: 1.8k stars; EverCrypt/HACL* code is used in Firefox NSS and other Project Everest artifacts
tradeoffs: Source is written in F*/Low*/Vale and compiled via KaRaMeL to C/assembly rather than hand-written C; gains formal proofs of memory safety, functional correctness and secret-independence (constant-time) at the cost of a heavy build toolchain (F*, KaRaMeL, Vale) compared to a plain C/asm library.
caveats: The paper's headline claim is mostly 'matches or exceeds' OpenSSL rather than a large win — the concrete beat documented with full methodology is only ~3% on this one primitive (Curve25519) on one 2017-era CPU. The same paper's AES-GCM/ChaCha20-Poly1305 figures (Figs. 7-8, i9-9900K) show EverCrypt's targeted implementation roughly matching OpenSSL's rather than clearly beating it, so do not extrapolate the 3% figure to other primitives. The actively-maintained home for production use has since moved to https://github.com/cryspen/hacl-packages.
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: HACL* GitHub README citation trail to the EverCrypt IEEE S&P'20 paper PDF (project-everest.github.io/assets/evercrypt.pdf), located after arXiv queries for 'verified cryptographic OpenSSL performance' surfaced only related/adjacent papers

name: AWS-LC
workload: Full TLS 1.2/1.3 handshake and session-resumption throughput (new connections/sec, via HAProxy) under an independent third-party benchmark
claimed_speedup: AWS-LC 1.29.0 (built with -DCMAKE_C_STANDARD=11) reached ~63,000 conn/s in the full-handshake test, beating OpenSSL 3.1-3.4 (~42,500) and OpenSSL 3.0.x (~21,000), roughly matching/exceeding OpenSSL 1.1.1 (~48,000); in the TLS-resumption test with HAProxy's lightweight locks it was the best overall performer at ~183,000 conn/s vs OpenSSL 1.1.1w's 124,000 and OpenSSL 3.0.2/3.0.14's ~7,000-8,000 conn/s

hardware: AWS r8g.16xlarge instance, 64 Graviton4 (ARM Neoverse V2) cores
stars_or_usage: 835 stars; used internally at AWS (s2n-tls, AWS SDKs, AWS-LC-rs) for TLS/crypto
tradeoffs: Code inherited from BoringSSL/OpenSSL retains original ISC/OpenSSL-era licensing alongside AWS-LC's own Apache-2.0/ISC files (mixed licensing across the tree); default build configuration silently underperforms until C11 is forced
caveats: Benchmark run and published by HAProxy (independent third party), not AWS; compiler version and optimization flags are not fully specified for every library in the comparison, only the C-standard build gotcha for AWS-LC.

name: picotls "fusion" AES-GCM engine
workload: AES-256-GCM AEAD encryption throughput for QUIC-sized short blocks (1440 bytes) compared to 16KB blocks
claimed_speedup: OpenSSL's AEAD throughput drops ~30% when encrypting 1440-byte blocks vs. 16KB blocks; picotls's 'fusion' engine cuts that short-block penalty to ~10% (derived from page data), i.e. fusion is meaningfully faster than OpenSSL specifically on QUIC-sized AEAD blocks
stars_or_usage: 641 stars; used in the H2O HTTP server
tradeoffs: Fusion is x86-64-specific and written in plain C (not hand assembly) to keep pipelines full for short AEAD blocks; it's one of four interchangeable crypto backends in picotls (OpenSSL, minicrypto, fusion, libaegis), so using it is opt-in and the OpenSSL backend remains the default for portability.
caveats: No CPU model or compiler flags are stated in the PR description, so this is capped at tier C rather than A/B. The chart gives only relative overhead percentages (not raw cycles/byte), and the OpenSSL version referenced (1.1.1g) is now several releases old.
found_via: GitHub README read for h2o/picotls, then opening its merged PR #310 ('"fusion" AES-GCM engine') which contains the benchmark writeup and graph

name: Tempesta FW (Tempesta TLS)
workload: Server-side full and abbreviated TLS 1.2 handshakes (ECDHE+ECDSA over NIST P-256) measured with the project's own tls-perf tool and wrk, comparing Nginx 1.19.1/OpenSSL 1.1.1d against Tempesta FW's in-Linux-kernel TLS handshake implementation, on a 1-vCPU KVM VM and on 2-node bare-metal servers
claimed_speedup: 40-80% more TLS connections/sec than Nginx/OpenSSL and up to 4x lower latency in some tests; concretely: 1-CPU VM new-session RPS 2,180 vs 1,545 (+41%), avg latency 307ms vs 1,340ms (-77%); 2-CPU bare-metal session-resumption 35,263 vs 19,203 conn/s (+83%); 2-CPU bare-metal new-session RPS only 7,921 vs 7,426 (+6%). Raw crypto op/s were slower than OpenSSL: ECDSA 27,261 vs OpenSSL's 36,472 op/s, ECDHE 6,690 vs OpenSSL's 16,619 op/s -- the throughput win comes from avoiding user/kernel context switches and heap allocation, not from faster math.
hardware: 1 vCPU KVM VM on Intel Core i7-6500U host (no vAPIC), virtio_net; 2-node bare-metal cluster with Intel Xeon E3-1240v5 CPUs and Mellanox ConnectX-2 10GbE, Linux kernel 5.7 (also compared to 4.14)
tradeoffs: Linux-kernel-only (x86-64 with AVX/BMI/ADX required, no generic C fallback for the crypto routines), puts TLS handshake code in kernel space (larger attack surface / TCB), GPLv2 licensing, and the paper itself reports tail-latency spikes up to 30x worse in the worst case on bare metal under SoftIRQ load
caveats: This is a first-party paper/benchmark by the Tempesta Technologies team (NetDev 0x14 workshop paper), not independent peer review, so it is capped at tier C despite public benchmark code (tls-perf) and stated hardware; compiler and build flags are not given; the headline 40-80% figure applies mainly to the VM scenario and to session resumption -- the bare-metal new-session improvement was only +6%; test hardware and kernel (5.7, 2020) are dated.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "tempesta" --sort stars; paper found via HN Algolia query "TLS faster than OpenSSL" -> https://netdevconf.info/0x14/pub/papers/35/0x14-paper35-talk-paper.pdf

name: brpc
workload: Same-machine and cross-machine RPC echo workloads: QPS vs request size, QPS vs thread count, and tail-latency CDFs under 1% long-tail requests, single-server and multi-hop server topologies
claimed_speedup: brpc reaches ~2.3GB/s throughput with pooled connections and dominates gRPC (protobuf/HTTP2, release-0.11) on QPS, multi-thread scaling, and tail latency in every scenario tested; gRPC 'is near the bottom of almost every test' and its latency CDF 'goes out of control' under cross-machine load with some requests timing out. Also beats Apache Thrift 0.9.1 on cross-machine average latency and matches/beats it on single-machine throughput once request size grows.
hardware: Single machine: dual E5-2620 24 logical cores, 64GB RAM; multi-machine clusters of E5-2420/E5-2620 v3 nodes with 1GbE/10GbE NICs (exact models given in doc)
tradeoffs: Historically closely tied to Baidu's internal protocols and tooling; heavier/more complex than lightweight RPC libs; primarily documented in Chinese.
caveats: The document itself states the tests were run in 2015 and 'may not reflect the latest status of the package'; gRPC tested was an ancient pre-1.0 release (release-0_11) which is not representative of modern gRPC (post-HTTP2-optimizations, post-1.0); compiler and build flags are not stated anywhere in the doc, only CPU models, so evidence is capped at C.
